newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-DMG looks for new chairman as Craven retires.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-DMG looks for new chairman as Craven retires.

text.p: Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank AG, said on Tuesday its chairman Sir John Craven would retire but that it has not yet singled out his successor.
The firm, which has been plagued by problems in its fund management arm, stressed Craven's departure was not related to difficulties in this area.
A DMG spokesman told Reuters that Craven would retire at the end of May but would join the advisory board of the Deutsche Bank group. He declined to comment on who might succeed Craven.
"That will be decided in due course," he said, adding that Craven "continues to be a close friend and colleague of the Deutsche Bank group".

The investment bank was quick to dispel suggestions in a British newspaper report that Craven's retirement from DMG was due to his disappointment at high-profile problems at fund management arm Morgan Grenfell Asset Management.

"His retirement has nothing whatsoever to do with the Peter Young affair as speculated in the press today," DMG spokesman Markus Will said. Tuesday's Daily Telegraph linked his departure with this and the controversial resignation of fund manager Nicola Horlick in January.

DMG's fund management arm, Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, is widely expected to be severely disciplined shortly by British investment watchdog the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) for problems in funds managed by Peter Young.

Fund manager Young was sacked by MGAM last September following the uncovering of irregularities in the funds. Young, who has said he is not guilty of any criminal activity, is currently under investigation by Britain's Serious Fraud Office.

The episode has been an embarrassing and costly one for DMG, which has aggressively been building up its investment banking business with the aim of joining key Wall Street firms as one of a handful of truly global banking giants.

DMG's parent Deutsche has already agreed to a record 200 million pound ($325 million) compensation package to retail investors in the funds, where suspect valuations of unlisted securities led to the bank making a 180 million pound cash injection.

In addition to an IMRO fine which some say could top the million pound mark, Deutsche will also have to bear the cost of IMRO's expenses in bringing the case, bills from both IMRO's and its own accounting and legal advisers and the bureaucratic costs of assessing individual losses among a possible total of 90,000 investors.

The fall-out of the highly-publicised departure of Horlick as head of MGAM's British pension fund business has not been so spectacular but it has further dented the confidence of institutions in the firm. Horlick resigned after being suspended for allegedly trying to take her team with her in a defection to Dutch financial services group ABN AMRO.
Craven, 56, was chief executive of Morgan Grenfell from 1987 to 1989 when he was made chairman of the group. Before this he founded mergers and acquisitions boutique Phoenix Securities.
He was previously deputy chairman of British merchant bank SG Warburg, which he joined in 1967.
Phoenix was bought by Morgan Grenfell in 1987 when it hired Craven as its chief executive. It regained its independence when Morgan Grenfell was bought by Deutsche in 1989 for 950 million pounds.
Craven was knighted last year and earlier this month was appointed as the new chairman of British conglomerate Lonrho Plc, a position he takes over from John Leahy on Wednesday.
He lists his recreations as hunting, shooting and skiing.
